title: Out-of-Distribution Graph Models Merging
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Models perform best when tested on their own training domain and degrade sharply on unseen domains, regardless of architecture.
layout: 3 side-by-side heatmap panels, left-to-right, red dashed boxes on the diagonal
description: Three side-by-side 3x3 heatmaps, labeled (a) GCN, (b) GAT and (c) GIN, show accuracy for different GNN backbones. In each panel the columns are the training domain (A, B, C) and the rows are the testing domain (A, B, C). Each cell holds a numeric accuracy value. The diagonal cells, where training and testing domains match, are outlined with red dashed boxes. They use warm red and pink shades and hold the highest values, roughly 60 to 76. Off-diagonal cells shade from light pink to lavender to deep purple and drop to about 42 to 60, with the lowest values near 50 or below when testing on an unseen domain. The eye goes first to the dark red top-left cell and the dashed diagonal. The pattern repeats across all three architectures.
caption: Comparison of different GNN models' generalization performance on PTC between in-distribution and OOD scenarios, with three domains represented as A / B / C. Values indicate Acc (%). The results within the red dashed box represent best performance.
abstract: This paper studies a novel problem of out-of-distribution graph models merging, which aims to construct a generalized model from multiple graph models pre-trained on different domains with distribution discrepancy. This problem is challenging because of the difficulty in learning domain-invariant knowledge implicitly in model parameters and consolidating expertise from potentially heterogeneous GNN backbones. In this work, we propose a graph generation strategy that instantiates the mixture distribution of multiple domains. Then, we merge and fine-tune the pre-trained graph models via a MoE module and a masking mechanism for generalized adaptation. Our framework is architecture-agnostic and can operate without any source/target domain data. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in addressing the model generalization problem.
